400.title: Metzora: the priest goes out (Leviticus 14:3)
400.hook: the priest goes outside the camp to the person, not the other way round
400.howItsDone: Visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is counted among the acts of kindness in Jewish law, and some synagogues and communities run bikur cholim groups that visit hospitals, homes and care facilities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cry from outside the camp, so that others would pray. Your line was pray for the one outside. Did you tell someone what you're carrying? Today, someone actually goes out there. Day four hundred.

Day four hundred. In our world, healing usually runs in one direction. You make the appointment. You find the parking. You sit in the waiting room with a clipboard. The sick person does the traveling, because that's where the expert is. The next portion, Metzora, opens with a person who has been living outside the camp with tzara'at. Maybe the mark has faded. Maybe they're ready to come home. But they aren't allowed back in to ask. So the Torah turns the usual direction around.
screen: `THE WAITING ROOM AND THE CLIPBOARD.` → `STUCK OUTSIDE THE CAMP.` → `THE DIRECTION TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Metzora means the afflicted one, the person with tzara'at. The whole portion is about their way back. Then the verse. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "the priest shall go forth out of the camp". The person can't come to the center. So the center comes to them. The priest, whose place is at the sanctuary, walks out past the last tent to where the outsider lives, and looks. Why does that matter? The priest's job here isn't only to judge. It's to be the bridge back. Some commentators notice that the person outside has no way to start their own return. Someone from inside has to make the first move. It feeds a whole tradition. Jewish law calls visiting the sick bikur cholim, and treats it as a duty, not a favor. The Talmud teaches that the Torah's command to walk after God means to copy God's ways: as God visited Abraham when he was recovering, so you visit the sick. Another passage says a visitor takes away a sliver of the sick person's suffering, one sixtieth. Not a cure. A sliver. But a real one. Some communities have a bikur cholim committee, people who go to hospitals and homes so no one is left alone. Notice the shape of today's verse: not the outsider going to the center, but the center going out. It's the same shape as a casserole on a doorstep, or a hospital visit on a weeknight.
screen: `METZORA: THE AFFLICTED ONE.` · `THE PRIEST GOES FORTH.` · `SOMEONE INSIDE MOVES FIRST.` · `BIKUR CHOLIM: VISITING THE SICK.` · then, large: `GO OUT TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go to someone who can't come to you. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who can't easily get to you right now. Someone sick, elderly, housebound, newly a parent, without a car, or just stuck. Picture where they are, and what their day looks like from there. Then plan the visit, or the call, or the small delivery. Put a day on it. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers until you go. The bell holds the time.
Metzora. The afflicted one: the portion that opens with the priest going out of the camp to them, not waiting for them to come in.
Your line: go out to them. Today, make the first move toward someone who can't come to you. Day four hundred.

what a scholar hears: Leviticus 14:3 sends the priest out of the camp; Sotah 14a grounds bikur cholim in imitating God, and Nedarim 39b gives the one-sixtieth teaching.

401.title: Metzora: cedar and hyssop (Leviticus 14:4)
401.hook: the tall cedar and the low hyssop; Rashi reads them as pride brought low
401.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often read the purification rites of Metzora as lessons in humility, following Rashi, and the portion is read in synagogue in the spring, often together with Tazria.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Metzora began with the priest walking out of the camp. Your line was go out to them. Did you make a first move toward someone? Today, what he carries with him. Day four hundred one.

Some objects are chosen for what they mean as much as for what they do. A wedding ring is just a circle of metal until it isn't. When the priest goes out to the person who may be healed, he asks for a strange little bundle. Two living birds. A piece of cedar wood. Some scarlet thread. And a sprig of hyssop. The Torah lists them without a word of explanation. Nobody in the text says why these four. So readers, from the ancient rabbis on, have kept asking.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF METAL.` → `BIRDS, CEDAR, SCARLET, HYSSOP.` → `WHY THESE FOUR?`

segments.voice: Start with the two plants. In the Bible the cedar is the great tree of Lebanon: Solomon built the Temple and his palace with its wood. Hyssop is the opposite: a small, low herb, growing out of cracks in walls. The book of Kings, describing Solomon's wisdom, says he spoke of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop on the wall. Top to bottom. The whole range. Then Rashi's reading. Rashi starts from the rabbis' teaching that afflictions came because of arrogance and harmful speech. So, he says, the cedar stands for the haughtiness that brought the trouble. And the cure? Let the person lower themselves from their pride, like the worm and like the hyssop. Then the worm. That's the scarlet thread. In Hebrew it's called the worm's scarlet, because the red dye came from a tiny insect. So the bundle holds one very tall thing and two very low ones. So what does the bundle say, in this reading? The way back into the camp runs downward. Not into shame: Rashi doesn't tell the person to hate themselves. Just smaller, closer to the ground. The person who once looked down on others, in this reading, comes home by remembering they're a creature among creatures. Some teachers also note the cedar stays in the bundle. Nobody throws it out. Height isn't the problem. Forgetting the hyssop is.
screen: `CEDAR HIGH, HYSSOP LOW.` · `RASHI: PRIDE BROUGHT LOW.` · `SCARLET FROM A WORM.` · `THE WAY BACK RUNS DOWNWARD.` · then, large: `FROM CEDAR TO HYSSOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lower yourself one notch. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you've been standing a little tall lately. An argument you needed to win. A group where you're quietly sure you're the smartest. A person you talk down to without meaning to. Picture yourself not falling, just stepping down one notch, eye to eye with them. What would you say differently from there? Notice how it feels to be hyssop for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Metzora. The portion where the way home is carried in a bundle of cedar, scarlet and hyssop: the tall brought low.
Your line: from cedar to hyssop. Today, in one conversation, let the other person be right about something, without adding a but. Day four hundred one.

402.title: Metzora: the bird set free (Leviticus 14:7)
402.hook: one bird is let go over the open field
402.howItsDone: The bird ritual of Leviticus 14 belonged to the Temple era and is not performed today; Jews study it in the weekly Torah reading, and some teachers draw lessons about speech and release from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Metzora, cedar and hyssop: the tall brought low. Your line was from cedar to hyssop. Did you let someone be right without adding a but? Today, the two birds in that bundle. Day four hundred two.

A bird trapped in a room panics against the glass. Then someone opens a window, and all at once it finds the gap and it's gone. Silence, and an open sky. The ritual for coming home from tzara'at has a moment like that. Outside the camp, the priest stands with the person who has been healed. Two small birds, alike. And only one of them will still be there at the end.
screen: `THE BIRD FINDS THE GAP.` → `TWO SMALL BIRDS, ALIKE.` → `ONLY ONE STAYS.`

segments.voice: Why birds at all? Rashi offers an answer: the affliction came from chattering, from careless speech, so the person brings birds, which chirp and twitter all day. The rite holds up a picture of the very thing that caused the trouble. Then the two fates. One bird is slaughtered over an earthen bowl of fresh running water. The living bird is dipped, along with the cedar, scarlet and hyssop, and the person is sprinkled seven times. Then the priest lets the living bird go, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "into the open field." Which way does it fly? The Mishnah adds a detail: the priest doesn't turn toward the sea, or toward the city, or toward the wilderness, but toward the open field, as the verse says. And what does the free bird mean? The Torah doesn't say, and readers have offered different answers. Some say the impurity is carried off and away. Some hear the person in the bird: someone who was shut outside, now released, flying back to life. And some teachers put the two birds side by side. The same kind of speech can wound, or it can sing. One bird is the old way of talking, ended. The other is the voice set free to start again. All of these are interpretations. What the text gives us is the picture itself: the priest's hands opening, and a small bird climbing over a field.
screen: `BIRDS, BECAUSE BIRDS CHATTER.` · `ONE OFFERED, ONE DIPPED.` · `TOWARD THE OPEN FIELD.` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY WHY.` · then, large: `LET THE BIRD GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing go. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're holding onto that's done its time: an old resentment, a story you keep retelling about yourself, a hurt that's already been answered. Picture it as a small bird in your cupped hands. Notice how tightly you're holding it. Then, on an out-breath, picture your hands opening, and the bird lifting toward an open field. You don't have to watch where it goes. The bell holds the time.
Metzora. The portion where, at the end of the healing rite, a living bird is set free over an open field.
Your line: let the bird go. Today, when an old grievance flies back into your head, open your hands, literally, and let it pass. Day four hundred two.

403.title: Metzora: empty the house first (Leviticus 14:33–36)
403.hook: even walls can be afflicted; the house is emptied first to spare the owner's things
403.howItsDone: The laws of afflicted houses are studied in the Mishnah's tractate Negaim and in the weekly reading of Metzora; the principle that the Torah has concern for people's property is cited in later Jewish law.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Metzora, a living bird flew free over an open field. Your line was let the bird go. Did you open your hands on an old grievance? Today, the affliction moves into the walls. Day four hundred three.

Black mold behind the bathroom tiles is its own kind of bad news. Something is wrong with the house itself, the place that was supposed to be safe. Leviticus 14 imagines something like it. A homeowner notices greenish or reddish streaks sunk into the stone. He goes to the priest and says, carefully, something like a plague has appeared in my house. Before the priest even steps through the door, the Torah gives an instruction that has nothing to do with stone at all.
screen: `MOLD BEHIND THE TILES.` → `STREAKS IN THE STONE.` → `BEFORE THE PRIEST GOES IN.`

segments.voice: Start with the instruction. The priest commands that the house be emptied before he goes in to look. Why? Because once he declares the house unclean, everything still inside becomes unclean with it. Then, whose sake it's for. The Mishnah asks what would be lost, and answers: clothes and wood can be washed or purified, but earthenware pots can't. They'd have to be broken. And the Mishnah draws a principle from that: the Torah has concern for people's property. Before it rules on the walls, it saves the dishes. Rashi adds a surprise. Rashi passes on an old midrash about why the walls were struck at all. The Amorites, it says, hid their gold in the walls of their houses during the forty years Israel was in the desert. A plague on the wall meant the stones came out, and the owner found treasure. An affliction that turns out to be a gift. It's a story, a midrash, not something the verse says. And an honest note. A rabbinic opinion in the Talmud says a plagued house never actually happened and never will; it was written to be studied. Other rabbis answered that they knew of places where it had. The sources disagree, and they leave the disagreement standing. Whichever view you take, the verse keeps its order: empty it first. Take care of what matters before the verdict, because the verdict, whatever it is, shouldn't destroy more than it has to.
screen: `EMPTY THE HOUSE BEFORE HE LOOKS.` · `SAVE THE CLAY POTS.` · `THE GOLD IN THE WALLS.` · `NEVER HAPPENED, OR DID IT?` · then, large: `EMPTY IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear out one corner. Settle, and breathe. Picture one corner of your home that's been quietly building up. A drawer, a closet shelf, the chair that collects clothes. Picture emptying it, item by item, onto the floor. Which things do you want to save? Which have you been keeping only because you never looked? Later today, if you can, go and actually do it. One corner, emptied first, then looked at with fresh eyes. The bell holds the time.
Metzora. The portion where even a house can be afflicted, and the priest has it emptied first, to spare the owner's things.
Your line: empty it first. Today, before you deal with a problem, take a minute to protect what doesn't need to be lost. Day four hundred three.

fork.setup: you're the priest. a homeowner reports streaks in his walls. what do you do first?

what a scholar hears: Mishnah Negaim 12:5 says the Torah has concern for Israel's property; Sanhedrin 71a records the view that a plagued house never was, and the reply that some knew where one stood.

404.title: Metzora: coming back in (Leviticus 14:8–9)
404.hook: washed and renewed, the person returns to the camp
404.howItsDone: Jewish tradition teaches teshuvah, return, as always possible; communities welcome people back after illness or estrangement, and someone recovered from serious illness may say Birkat Hagomel, a blessing of thanks, at the Torah reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Metzora, the house was emptied before the priest looked. Your line was empty it first. Did you protect something before tackling a problem? Today, the last steps home. Day four hundred four.

Coming back is its own kind of hard. The first day at work after a long illness. Walking into a family dinner after a year of not speaking. Stepping out of prison, or rehab, or a hospital, into a world that kept going without you. It's awkward. Where do you sit? Leviticus has been following a person outside the camp for two chapters now. The priest came out. The bird flew free. And now the Torah does something careful: it doesn't just open the gate. It walks them back in, step by step.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY BACK.` → `WHERE DO I SIT?` → `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: It starts with washing. The person washes their clothes, shaves their hair, and bathes in water. Twice in two verses the Hebrew says ve-taher, and he shall be clean. Then they come into the camp. Then, not all at once. Even inside, they stay outside their own tent for seven more days. On the seventh day they shave again, head, beard and eyebrows, wash again, bathe again. Coming back takes a week. The Torah doesn't pretend re-entry is a single moment. Then the eighth day. Back in Tzav, sixteen days ago on this path: when the priests were ordained, blood was placed on the right ear, the right thumb, the right big toe. Listen, do, walk. Now, in Leviticus 14, the same three places are touched on the person who has just come back. Blood, and then oil, on ear, thumb and toe. The one who was outside the camp is marked the way the priests were marked. Some readers hear it this way: not as damaged goods, but as someone beginning again. And the way back has a name. Jewish tradition calls returning teshuvah, and it insists the door is never fully shut. Maimonides writes that a person who returns should not think they are far from the virtue of the righteous. Leviticus 14 makes that a ritual: the person who was outside the camp ends up marked like a priest. Hair grows back. Clothes are washed. There is a way back, and it has steps.
screen: `VE-TAHER: AND HE SHALL BE CLEAN.` · `SEVEN DAYS OUTSIDE HIS TENT.` · `EAR, THUMB, TOE, LIKE A PRIEST.` · `TESHUVAH: THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `THERE IS A WAY BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone back. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has been away, by illness, by a mistake, by a falling-out, and is trying to come back in. A coworker returning from leave. A relative who messed up. A friend who went quiet. Picture their first awkward moment back. Now picture yourself making it easier: a greeting, a seat saved, a normal question. Not a speech. A step. The bell holds the time.
Metzora. The portion that walks the afflicted person back into the camp, step by step, and marks them on ear, thumb and toe like a priest.
Your line: there is a way back. Today, make one small gesture of welcome to someone returning, or allow yourself one step back toward someone. Day four hundred four.

405.title: Acharei Mot: after the deaths (Leviticus 16:1)
405.hook: the Yom Kippur service is given right after Aaron's loss
405.howItsDone: In traditional synagogues, Leviticus 16 is read on Yom Kippur morning, and Ashkenazi communities recite Yizkor, the memorial prayer for the dead, on Yom Kippur and on the pilgrimage festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Metzora ended with a person walked home, step by step. Your line was there is a way back. Did you make one small gesture of welcome? Today, a new portion that looks back before it looks forward. Day four hundred five.

Some dates in a family's calendar carry two things at once. A wedding planned for the month after a funeral. A holiday that falls on the anniversary of a loss. They can't be separated, and after a while families stop trying. The next portion of Leviticus is called Acharei Mot, after the death. It's where the Torah lays out the service for Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. And it doesn't begin with the day, or the rules. It begins by reaching back six chapters, to Aaron's terrible day.
screen: `TWO THINGS ON ONE DATE.` → `ACHAREI MOT: AFTER THE DEATH.` → `BACK TO AARON'S LOSS.`

segments.voice: Start with the opening. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God spoke to Moses "after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before the LORD, and died." Chapters of skin, birth and houses have come in between. But the Torah ties the Day of Atonement back to Nadav and Avihu. Why mention the deaths here? Rashi compares it to two doctors visiting a sick man. The first says: don't eat cold food, don't lie in a damp place. The second says the same, and adds: so you don't die the way so-and-so died. The second warning lands harder. The rules for entering the holy place are given with the memory of the sons still fresh. Grief and atonement sit side by side. The Jerusalem Talmud asks why the deaths of Aaron's sons are placed next to Yom Kippur, and answers that the death of the righteous, like Yom Kippur, brings atonement. Whatever one makes of that, it's a striking pairing: loss doesn't sit outside the holy day. It's written into its first line. And here is how it's lived. In traditional synagogues, this very chapter is read on Yom Kippur morning. And on Yom Kippur, Ashkenazi communities say Yizkor, the memorial prayer for those they've lost. The Day of Atonement makes room for the dead. After grief, atonement. Not instead of grief. After it, and with it.
screen: `AFTER THE DEATH OF AARON'S SONS.` · `RASHI: THE SECOND DOCTOR'S WARNING.` · `LOSS IN THE FIRST LINE.` · `YIZKOR ON YOM KIPPUR.` · then, large: `AFTER GRIEF, ATONEMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one grief teach you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a loss you've carried. A person, a time of life, a hope that didn't happen. Don't rush past the sadness of it. Then ask, gently: what has this loss taught me? About what matters, about how I treat people, about what I'd do differently now? If nothing comes, that's all right. Grief teaches on its own schedule. If you pray, you can remember the one you lost in your prayers. The bell holds the time.
Acharei Mot. After the death: the portion that gives the Yom Kippur service, and begins with Aaron's loss.
Your line: after grief, atonement. Today, when an old sadness comes up, let it stay a moment, and ask what it's asking of you. Day four hundred five.

fork.reveal: the Torah begins with the deaths: after the death of the two sons of Aaron. grief is in the first line of the holy day.

trapdoor: what you thought: the start of the Yom Kippur rules.
what it means: the Day of Atonement is introduced through loss, and keeps a place for grief.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 16:1 gives the two-doctors parable; the Jerusalem Talmud (Yoma 1:1) sets the death of the righteous beside Yom Kippur as atoning.

406.title: Acharei Mot: not at all times (Leviticus 16:2)
406.hook: even the high priest may enter the holiest place only once a year
406.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, the Musaf service in traditional synagogues retells the high priest's service in the holy of holies, called the Avodah, and Shabbat rest is another limit that sets time apart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Acharei Mot began with Aaron's loss. Your line was after grief, atonement. Did an old sadness get to stay a moment? Today, the first rule of the Day of Atonement, and the end of a week. Day four hundred six.

We live in an age of always. Stores open all night. Messages that arrive at three in the morning. Every show, every song, every person, a tap away, any hour. The idea that something should be off limits most of the time can feel almost foreign. The first instruction Moses receives for Yom Kippur isn't about what Aaron should do. It's about what he shouldn't. The high priest, who wears the golden plate engraved holy to the LORD, is told there's a room he may not simply walk into.
screen: `OPEN ALL NIGHT.` → `THE FIRST RULE IS A NO.` → `A ROOM HE CAN'T WALK INTO.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: tell Aaron "that he come not at all times into the holy place within the veil." Behind that curtain is the holy of holies, the ark and its cover. Then the limit. The chapter goes on to describe one day, the tenth of the seventh month, when the high priest goes in, with incense and blood, on behalf of everyone. Only that day. Some readers draw a lesson: the closer you are to the center, the more the limits matter. There's care inside the limit, too. The Mishnah describes the high priest coming out of the holy of holies and saying a short prayer in the outer room. Short, it says, so as not to frighten the people waiting outside. The limit isn't coldness. Everyone outside is holding their breath for him. Look at the week behind us. Metzora opened with the priest going out of the camp. Then cedar and hyssop, a bird set free, a house emptied before the verdict, and a person walked home step by step. Acharei Mot began with grief before atonement. And now: not at all times. Jewish life is full of these boundaries. Shabbat closes the week's work at sundown. Some things are kept for one night a year. Some find the limit is what keeps the thing precious. A door you can open any time can stop being a door.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one limit. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that would mean more if it weren't available all the time. Your phone at the dinner table. A favorite food. Work email after dark. A certain conversation you keep reopening. Choose one limit you could keep, just for today, or just for this evening. Picture the door closing, gently, and what might have room to grow on the other side of it. The bell holds the time.
Acharei Mot. The portion where even the high priest may enter the holiest place only on one day a year.
Your line: not at all times. Tonight, keep one limit you chose, and notice what it protects. Day four hundred six, and another week of Leviticus behind you.
